# Nutrition: deficit, surplus, protein, supplements

Two fundamental rules of body transformation: (1) energy balance (deficit/surplus), (2) sufficient protein + lifting. **Dieting without lifting = losing muscle along with fat** — don't hand out a fat-loss plan without a training component.

## 1. Calories: calibration instead of formulas

- Formulas (Mifflin, etc.) are only a starting estimate. The reliable method: **log everything eaten + weigh in every morning for at least 2 weeks**. Weight steady → the logged macros = maintenance. Recalibrate maintenance periodically (it changes with weight, activity, training volume).
- **Deficit: −25% from maintenance** (default), range 15–35% by circumstance. ~3 months of deficit → visible changes.
- **A minimum allowable calorie level exists**: below it isn't faster — it's loss of strength, microtears, muscle loss. Symptoms of failure: strength dropping in the gym, "something aches" → raise calories.
- **Surplus: +5–10%**, no more — a large surplus doesn't speed up a natural's muscle growth, only fat ("dirty bulking isn't relevant", the composition of what's gained is ~50/50 muscle/fat even at a small surplus).
- Accuracy of ±100 kcal/day is enough; plan adjustments — in steps of ≥150 kcal.
- Activity is a powerful lever: 15,000–20,000 steps/day let you eat noticeably more. But 3 sessions/week don't earn the right to eat 5000.

### Typical counting mistakes (warn in advance)
- Cooked vs dry (rice: 170 vs 340 kcal/100 g; "cooked buckwheat" vs 50 g dry).
- Without a kitchen scale, "by eye" diverges from reality; macros are "per serving" on labels.
- Meat fat content: you don't see fat with your eyes → so it's not there; the visual scale is more accurate than the label.
- App databases are inconsistent → **log only macros, compute calories by formula from the macros**.
- Cafes are the #1 source of errors (soups are the worst). The palm method is a valid rough alternative; counting is more reliable.

## 2. Protein

- **1.6 g/kg** — the baseline for trainees (meta-analyses); **1.8–2.0** — with a margin; **2.2** — with extra activity; up to **2.5** — under large combined load.
- With lots of excess fat, count **from target weight** (normal BMI). Typical absolutes: women ~90–100 g, men ~140–180 g.
- Overshooting isn't dangerous with healthy kidneys ("protein kills the kidneys" is a myth for the healthy; contraindicated only with kidney disease).
- **Distribution: 3–4 even portions per day.** Timing is meaningless for beginners (anabolic window up to ~3 days). For experienced lifters on a plateau: ~2/3 of protein around/after training, ~20 g 1–2 h before. Timing data is contradictory — present it as optional optimization.
- Quality: any animal source has a complete amino profile. **Collagen as a protein source is useless.** Plant: ½ legumes + ¼ grains + ¼ seeds, amount ×1.5 (absorption ~2/3); pea+rice ≈ whey.
- Variety of sources = micronutrients: dairy → calcium; red meat → B12, creatine, heme iron, zinc; seafood → iodine/minerals; plants → fiber. Protein powder is protein without vitamins — don't replace half the diet with it.
- Satiety: egg white is the most filling; liquid protein lasts 1–1.5 hours. **Cottage cheese is the slowest protein** (200–400 g = an ~8 h "drip", good at night).

## 3. Fats and carbs

- Demonizing any macronutrient is baseless. **Fats ≥30 g/day always** (gallstone risk at zero). **Women need more fat**: low fat/large deficit → menstrual disruption/loss (reversible but serious).
- The spectrum of fats: omega-3 → omega-6 → unsaturated → healthy saturated (fish, avocado, olives, nuts, seeds; whole coconut, dark chocolate). A healthy spectrum improves the lipid profile without drugs. Butter is hard to account for; default to excluding it or dosing strictly (~5 g for frying).
- Carbs: not below ~40–50 g/day (the ketosis threshold). The quality criterion of a source is **not "speed" but what else is inside**: fruit — fast, but with fiber and vitamins → healthy; white bread — "slow" but empty. Buckwheat is the best cut-phase side (volume, fiber, B vitamins, low calorie density).
- Carbs in the evening — a weak positive effect in meta-analyses: don't sweat it and don't forbid it.
- Keto is a legitimate tool **only** for appetite control; for some people it doesn't fit at all. Any "cult" (keto/carnivore/IF) works through a hidden deficit and individual predisposition.

## 4. Satiety — the key to holding a deficit

- **Fullness is determined by food volume, not calories** (experimentally: a 1000 kcal deficit in an iso-volume gel isn't detected). So: **on a cut, swap foods for less calorie-dense ones, don't shrink portions**.
- Tools: vegetables/mushrooms (volume at ~100 kcal a plate), psyllium (thickens yogurt), fiber or fat in a meal slows absorption of everything, shirataki/bran ≈ 0 kcal.
- Flexibility > rigidity: occasional cafe meals are fine, "90% of the time on plan" is enough. Rigid bans and fanatical counting → breakdowns and disordered-eating patterns (especially in women). Danger-zone signs: fear of food, 90% of thoughts about food, dropping social life → soften the approach, switch the goal from "leanness" to "strength".

## 5. Bulk/cut cycles

- Long-term muscle maximum: **2/3–3/4 of the time on a bulk** (surplus +5–10%, trend visible over 1–2 months, bump calories in small steps), **cuts kept short** with a bigger deficit at the start and smaller at the end (lower body fat % → higher risk of muscle loss).
- Mistakes #1 and #2: too aggressive a bulk ("got smothered in fat") and an endless cut (muscle doesn't grow).
- Beach reference ~10–12% body fat; the exact % can't be measured and isn't needed — the mirror.
- An aggressive mini-cut ≤20 days is a working tool, but expert opinions diverge (present it with a caveat).
- Before a cut — at least a few months of bulking. On short cuts weight bounces with water and glycogen — fat can't be counted precisely.
- A fixed "natural ceiling" isn't proven, but each kg comes harder; the natural's path is very long, smooth bulks in the ~10–20% body-fat corridor. PEDs for an amateur are a "super crappy deal" (risks ≫ benefit); a coach offering PEDs to a beginner is a red flag.

## 6. Supplements

| Supplement | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Creatine | Works: +a few % to strength → more muscle over years. There are non-responders; the effect is stronger in those eating little meat |
| Caffeine | Works: stimulant + mild appetite suppression |
| Protein, omega-3, vitamins, calcium | Not "supplements" but compensation for diet gaps (calcium — if no dairy) |
| BCAA | Useless with sufficient protein (many tests) |
| Collagen | Useless as protein (3 non-essential amino acids) |
| Ashwagandha | Speculative: almost all studies are from India, low quality |

- Rule for evaluating supplement studies: look at who funded it (magnesium from a magnesium maker); wait for independent replication.

## 7. Tracking progress

- **Weight: daily in the morning, evaluate only the average trend over ≥2 weeks** — individual points are noisy with water/glycogen at ±2 kg.
- **Women: compare weight/photos in the same phase of the cycle** (up to +2 kg of water).
- Additionally: photos, girths (waist for cutting), clothes, caliper folds; a food and training diary is the basis for adjustments (strength dropping → deficit too large).
- "Fast/slow metabolism" is a half-myth: the difference between extreme percentiles is ~600 kcal; "eats and doesn't gain" = metabolism + low appetite.

## Sources
Meta-analyses on protein (1.6 g/kg), satiety studies (isocaloric gel), injury rate ~0.3/1000 hours, Barbell Medicine ("barbell therapy" for diagnoses). Podcast source: Podlodka #399 (Stas, evidence-based fitness).
